newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street and Eurobourses slide, dollar lower.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street and Eurobourses slide, dollar lower.

text.p: A fresh bout of market nerves that Wall Street's record-breaking run could be faltering depressed share prices worldwide on Wednesday and undermined the dollar.

Reviving fears of the red ink that washed over markets late last week, Wall Street, the world's biggest stock exchange, opened with pronounced losses. It then recovered some ground on wary bargain-hunting but slid again later.

The Dow Jones industrial average of U.S. blue-chips was down more than 115 points, or 1.8 percent, in late morning in New York. Key European stock markets had earlier ended well into the minus column but above their lows.
"We didn't get a meltdown today but we're not out of the woods yet," said Kirit Shah, strategist at Sanwa International in London, Europe's leading stock market.
"The only consolation is that since we haven't risen as much this year as Wall Street, we probably won't fall as far", one London trader said.

Market participants have fretted that the Dow, which has advanced by nearly a third this year, could be headed for a major correction. The London market's FTSE 100 index has risen by around nine percent in 1996, a third of the Dow's rate.

Dealers said concern that Japanese investors might trim holdings of U.S. stocks and bonds piled on the pressure and raised a question mark over recent strength in top shares, particularly technology stocks.
"People are looking for an excuse to sell," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management in New York. "Investors are extremely nervous."

Wall Street was also jolted by rumours that computer giant IBM was about to issue a profits warning. An IBM spokesman declined comment on the rumours but said the group had no plans for a news release on Wednesday.

A column in the Wall Street Journal had prompted jitters in Asian and European markets, well before New York opened, questioning whether Japanese financial institutions were losing interest in U.S. Treasuries. This also sent bond prices lower.

Concern that Japanese and other investors could cut their holdings of U.S. assets also undermined market sentiment for the dollar, analysts said. In addition, the U.S. currency was jolted by a widening of Japan's trade surplus with the United States.

"A lot of the overnight excuses for this profit-taking in the asset markets were pretty flimsy but there are some reasons to be nervous at this time of the year and so people are being cautious," said Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe.
The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip stocks in London, Europe's leading stock market, lost more than 70 points at one stage but ended down just over 50, or 1.3 percent.
The Paris bourse finished around 1.7 percent lower, while Frankfurt was down about 1.9 percent in late computerised trading amid investor concern that Wall Street might be facing a major correction.

In two days of recovery in share prices on Monday and Tuesday, stocks had clawed their way back from sharp losses at the end of last week after remarks by U.S. central bank chief Alan Greenspan on the "irrational exuberance" of Wall Street.

On the data front, U.S. wholesale prices provided few surprises. The November producer price index rose 0.4 percent, matching October's increase, but the core rate, excluding the volatile food and energy sectors, rose 0.1 percent after a 0.3 percent drop in October.

In other news, the Bank of England signalled no change in official interest rates on Wednesday after a monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted at 112.90 yen and 1.5410 marks against 113.29 and 1.5539 in late European business on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS CLOSING INDICES
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares ended 53.2 points lower at 3,982.5.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed bourse floor trade down 49.95 at 2,841.05 and was at 2.836.36 in late computerised trade. In Paris, the CAC-40 index ended down 38.12 at 2,213.28.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended at $368.65 an ounce, up 40 cents, after earlier rising to about $370. Silver rose two cents to $4.83.
